@@31532164 <h> A divided country hardens its stances <p> A divided country grew more divided in 2019 , as political warfare escalated , first over the release of a report on Russian interference in the 2016 election and then over impeachment hearings into whether President Trump pressured Ukraine to investigate his political rivals . <p> Rancor spread beyond Washington to the nation 's southern border , where the immigration debate intensified as migrants fleeing Central America were caught up in the president 's crackdown on illegal immigration and demands for a border wall . The political struggle over the wall led to the longest government shutdown in U.S. history . <p> Unified by their loathing of Trump , Democrats were fractured themselves as more than two dozen battled for their party 's 2020 presidential nomination . The issue will be settled by rapidly approaching Democratic primaries . <p> Division spread beyond the Atlantic and Pacific oceans , as the president 's trade war with China dented the economies of both countries , as well as the already slumping economies of Germany , France and Japan . China faced more turmoil as its bid for tighter control over Hong Kong sparked furious protests in the economically vital city . <p> Trump 's decision to withdraw U.S. forces from Syria over the objection of top military advisers drew bipartisan opposition in Congress to a move that threw the region into chaos and unraveled U.S. policy in the Mideast . The withdrawal overshadowed a daring U.S. commando raid that killed Abu Bakr al-Baghdadi , leader of the vicious Islamic State . <p> Mass shootings continued to plague the country and the world . Wildfires remained a constant threat in California , where power companies were forced to shut off electricity in an often futile attempt to prevent the fires , while debate raged over who is to blame . <p> A fire heavily damaged the iconic Notre Dame Cathedral in Paris , shocking the world , while the crash of two Boeing 737 Max jetliners called into question U.S. aviation safety practices . <p> Here are the top 10 national and international news stories of 2019 : <h> Constitutional clash <p> As the year began , the words " Mueller " and " Russia " dominated the headlines . As it ended , " impeachment " and " quid pro quo " took their place as controversy further engulfed the Trump administration . <p> In March , special counsel Robert Mueller submitted his report on Russian interference in the 2016 U.S. presidential election and allegations of coordination between Trump 's campaign and the Russians . Trump claimed exoneration as the report did not find sufficient evidence that his campaign " coordinated or conspired " with the Russian government as it interfered in the election . <p> Democrats howled as the report also called Russian interference -- mainly through hacking and fake social media stories -- illegal , " sweeping and systematic " yet welcomed by Trump 's campaign . It identified links between Trump officials and individuals with ties to the Russian government about which persons involved in the campaign lied or obstructed investigators . <p> Demands by leftist Democrats for Trump 's impeachment soon faded -- until reports of a July 25 call between Trump and Ukraine 's new president added more fuel to the impeachment fires . <p> Weeks of hearings by congressional Intelligence and Judicial committees culminated in partisan House votes on Dec. 18 to impeach Trump on two articles charging abuse of power and obstruction of Congress . Democrats who control the House accused Trump of pressuring Ukraine for political gain in a " quid pro quo " for the release of vitally needed military aid and blocking the House 's attempt to investigate . The move makes Trump only the fourth president in U.S. history to be brought to the brink of removal from office . <p> Political passions will flare early next year as Trump stands trial in the Senate . The impeachment effort will face an uphill battle in the Republican-led Senate , where a two-thirds vote would be needed to convict Trump and oust him from office . Analysts consider that an unlikely scenario in an election year . <h> Immigration <p> A U.S. Border Patrol agent stands near a section of privately built border wall under construction on Dec. 11 near Mission , Texas . ( John Moore/Getty Images ) <p> As he as done since taking office , Trump pressed efforts to curb legal and illegal immigration through executive orders and construction of 450 miles of barriers at the southwestern border . He also sought to cut down on the number of people who claim asylum in the U.S. Images of detained migrant children locked in cells at border stations galvanized opposition to Trump 's policies . <p> In September , the Supreme Court backed Trump , saying that the administration could block most Central American migrants from seeking asylum in the U.S. if they passed through another country and were not denied asylum there . That followed the court 's July ruling that the Trump administration could use $2.5 billion in Pentagon funds -- meant to combat drug trafficking -- to build a barrier along the border . <p> But in November , the Supreme Court said it would review a controversial Trump policy , blocked by lower courts , to end the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals program started by President Obama in 2012 . DACA aims to halt the deportation of young immigrants brought to the U.S. illegally . <p> Trump 's immigration policies also ran into legal roadblocks thrown up by Democratic attorneys general nationwide . In October , judges in four states barred his administration from trying to withhold green cards from people using public benefits and rejected his plan to use other funds to build the border wall . <p> The immigration war led to the longest government shutdown in U.S. history , from Dec. 22 , 2018 , to Jan. 25 , 2019 . The 35-day shutdown stemmed from an impasse over Trump 's demand in an appropriations bill for $5.7 billion to build the border wall . It ended when Trump agreed to a stopgap bill that did n't include funds for the wall . He later declared a national emergency to bypass Congress and fund the wall . <h> Dueling Democrats <p> As of mid-December , Democrats had reduced their field of major presidential contenders to 15 -- but not the intensity of the combat that raged nearly all year . <p> Former New York City Mayor Michael Bloomberg jumped into the race on Nov. 24 . Once seen as a strong contender , former Rep. Beto O'Rourke dropped out in early November , while another leading candidate , Sen. Kamala Harris , quit Dec. 3 . <p> Bloomberg bills himself as a pragmatic Democrat who can beat Trump . But his late entry roiled the primary field as moderate contenders like former Vice President Joe Biden and South Bend , Ind. , Mayor Pete Buttigieg dueled with progressives like Sens . Elizabeth Warren and Bernie Sanders on the campaign trail and in televised debates . Sen. Amy Klobuchar moved to the center but remained in the back of the pack with Sen. Cory Booker and others . <p> Not wanting to be overshadowed by the House impeachment hearings , the Democratic contenders focused mainly on health care . Progressives embraced a single-payer , Medicare-for-All health care program , while moderates argued for improving the current system based on the Affordable Care Act and private insurance . Early polling in the bellwether states of Iowa and New Hampshire favored moderate contenders . <h> Trade battles <p> Investors and manufacturers had been hoping for a resolution to the U.S.-China trade war by early 2019 , but as the year drew to a close , they had to settle for a " phase one deal " in which China agreed to increase some imports in exchange for the U.S. delaying an increase in tariffs on Chinese goods . Markets rebounded at the end of the year , even though the deal did n't address the major grievances the U.S. and other countries have with China : theft of technology and unfair trade practices . <p> Analysts feared that any short-term deal would be political window dressing with little economic impact , and that in the long term , the U.S.-China trade war may be unresolvable , further damaging U.S. manufacturers . <p> As Trump was pushing for a China trade deal , the House on Dec. 19 passed the U.S.-Mexico-Canada Agreement , signed a year ago by Trump and the leaders of Canada and Mexico to replace the Clinton-era North American Free Trade Agreement . The USMCA deal modernizes trade rules between the three countries and includes tougher labor and environmental standards sought by Democrats . It was expected to boost manufacturing in all three countries . The Senate was expected to take up the agreement in January . <h> Hong Kong protests <p> A proposal in June by Hong Kong 's government to allow extraditions to mainland China -- seen as a bid by Beijing to limit the city 's freedoms and autonomy -- has triggered continued protests and created another flashpoint between the U.S. and China . <p> Hong Kong 's government has withdrawn the proposal , but protesters still demand an investigation of harsh police tactics and pro-democracy reforms . Some have called for an end to the Chinese Communist Party , outraging Beijing . After a bipartisan push in Congress , Trump on Nov. 27 signed a bill designed to support the pro-democracy protesters . <p> China views the protests as a U.S. attempt to foment " revolution " in Hong Kong . The conflict threatens to increase not only economic but military tensions between the countries if China decides to challenge the U.S. Navy in the South China Sea . <h> Disarray in Mideast <p> Despite the killing of brutal ISIS leader Abu Bakr al-Baghdadi in a daring raid by U.S. special forces in northern Syria , doubts grew over U.S. policy and alliances in the Mideast . <p> On Oct. 27 , Trump announced that Baghdadi had blown himself up during the raid . Any political gain for the president , however , evaporated amid questions about Trump 's Oct. 6 order to withdraw all U.S. forces from Syria , where they had been supporting the fight against Islamic militants . <p> Trump ordered the pullout against the advice of top military advisers , one of whom he called " the world 's most overrated general . " Their prediction of ensuing chaos in the region was fulfilled when Turkey quickly launched a ferocious attack on Kurds , U.S. allies in the region . Russia boosted its forces in Syria , bolstering its ally -- dictator Bashar Assad -- and occupied U.S. bases there . <p> In November , Trump partially reversed his pullout order , saying the U.S. would keep 500 troops in the country and was committed to defeating ISIS . But allies in the region , like Israel , worried that Trump might again change Mideast policy without any consultation . <h> More mass shootings <p> A father hugs his daughter after being reunited after a shooting at Saugus High School that left two students dead and three wounded on Nov. 14 , 2019 . ( Mario Tama/Getty Images ) <p> Mass shootings have occurred across the country with increasing frequency in recent years , and 2019 was no exception . <p> On Nov. 14 , a student in Santa Clarita , Calif. , fatally shot two high school classmates before taking his own life . It was the fifth mass shooting at a school or school event this year . Overall , 404 mass shootings were cataloged by the Gun Violence Archive in 2019 , as of Monday . <p> After last summer 's back-to-back shootings in El Paso , Texas , and Dayton , Ohio , left 32 people dead , Trump vowed to take action but backed down under pressure from the National Rifle Association . Instead , the administration backed legislation to tackle gun violence by helping law enforcement partnerships to better use existing gun laws . <p> Firearms businesses faced growing pressure to curb gun violence . In October , Dick 's Sporting Goods destroyed more than $5 million worth of semi-automatic rifles and said it was considering ending gun sales . In September , Walmart said it would stop selling ammunition that could be used in assault rifles and Colt , the gunmaker , said it would effectively suspend production of sporting rifles for the civilian market . <p> In a potentially significant case , the Supreme Court in November allowed relatives of shooting victims at the Sandy Hook Elementary School to sue the Remington Arms Co. , the maker of the rifle used in that 2012 massacre . <p> American-style mass shootings spread to the rest of world . On March 15 , a racist gunman killed 51 people at two mosques in Christchurch , New Zealand , prompting a swift ban on assault rifles there . <h> California wildfires <p> Political conflict flared as wildfires , blamed on climate change , again raged across California this fall . The fires , which have killed 85 people and caused billions of dollars in damage over the past three years , this year have consumed more than 281,000 acres and forced thousands of Californians to flee their homes . <p> Although less destructive and deadly than the past two years , the fires still had a big impact . Planned blackouts , meant to prevent wildfires , also kept up to 3 million Californians without power in November and risked the health of many needing electricity for vital medical devices . <p> As he did after wildfires in 2018 , Trump blasted the state 's readiness to confront fires . Conservatives blamed environmentalists for the buildup of small trees and brush that fueled the blazes , while liberals pointed to fossil fuels , corporate ineptitude -- particularly by the bankrupt Pacific Gas &amp; Electric Co. -- and suburban sprawl into areas vulnerable to wildfires. <h> 737 Max crashes <p> Boeing 's top-selling 737 Max jetliner remains grounded after crashes in October 2018 and last March killed 346 people in the Java Sea and Ethiopia . The crashes were blamed on malfunctioning anti-stall software and poor pilot training , prompting questions about the Federal Aviation Administration 's process for certifying aircraft and about whether Boeing rushed production to meet orders for 5,000 of the jets . <p> The grounding has disrupted the aviation industry worldwide and plunged Boeing into the biggest crisis it has ever faced . The largest manufacturing exporter in the U.S. , Boeing has lost 15% of its stock value , and its CEO was ousted on Monday . Even after months of work by Boeing and federal aviation regulators , the 737 Max will remain grounded at least until late January and probably longer . <p> Last week , Boeing announced it will shut down Max production in January , resulting in sweeping job losses at Boeing and its suppliers . <h> Notre Dame fire <p> Smoke and flames rise during a fire at the landmark Notre-Dame Cathedral in central Paris on April 15 , 2019 . ( FRANCOIS GUILLOT/AFP via Getty Images ) <p> Flames engulfed Notre Dame cathedral in Paris on April 15 when a fire broke out beneath the historic structure 's roof . By the time it was put out , the cathedral 's spire and most of its roof had been destroyed and its upper walls heavily damaged . However , the three iconic 13th-century rose windows suffered little or no damage . Still , authorities said , the cathedral came close to collapsing . <p> Months after the fire spewed 460 tons of lead from Notre Dame 's ancient roof and spire across Paris , alarming amounts of the toxic metal -- up to 20 times safe levels on the left bank of the Seine -- were found despite decontamination efforts . French authorities were accused of covering up or neglecting the problem , and city fire officials were criticized for poor response times and communications in fighting the blaze . <p> Because of the damage , no Christmas services were held at the cathedral this year for the first time in nearly two centuries .

@@31532474 <h> Menu <p> The Friday Cover is POLITICO Magazine 's email of the week 's best , delivered to your inbox every Friday morning . <p> Email <p> By signing up you agree to receive email newsletters or alerts from POLITICO . You can unsubscribe at any time . This site is protected by reCAPTCHA and the Google Privacy Policy and Terms of Service apply . <p> James Bennet , the editor of the New York Times editorial page , lately has been waging his share of battles , which he no doubt would be enjoying more if he did not give a damn about rude things combatants say about him and his publication . <p> But he does give a damn . <p> Story Continued Below <p> Bennet , whom I 've known since we were both covering Bill Clinton 's White House , has faced a succession of social media uproars over the past year as he revamps and modernizes the Times opinion section . Even as the page has retained its historically liberal bearings , and regularly lacerates President Donald Trump , it is now regarded with suspicion by some loud voices on the left . There was a backlash to Bennet 's hiring of conservative columnist Bret Stephens ( who wrote skeptically about the evidence for manmade climate change ) , as well as to his abortive attempt to bring on tech writer Quinn Norton ( the hiring was quickly reversed after Twitter posters exposed a friendship with a neo-Nazi ) . These and other moves by Bennet to enliven his pages caused such intense distress by some at the Times that , in recent months , he met with a group of aggrieved colleagues -- the transcript of which later leaked -- and wrote an all-staff memo that explained his philosophy of debate . <p> For Bennet , giving a damn is a trap of sorts . His tenure has been about standing strong on behalf of a style of discourse that requires making points with precision , insists on the distinction between honest argument and propaganda , and defaults to an assumption that the other side has a legitimate point of view and is deserving of respect ... even when that other side is reveling in its contempt toward people who disagree . <p> So , do the critics bother him ? " Look , I do n't like to be called a Nazi , " Bennet said in a recent interview with Politico Magazine in his Times office . <p> Then , immediately , he seemed to realize that this sounded too much like the kind of hyperventilating , name-calling language some critics use against him and Times colleagues . " I should subtract that , " he quickly added . " I 've been told I 've been called a Nazi ; I have n't seen it . I should n't say that . " ( He has been called a Nazi sympathizer on social media . ) <p> " I do n't know that anybody likes to be screamed at , " he continued . " Maybe there are people , but I 'm not one of them . And I take it seriously . ... Our posture is that we do n't have all the answers . " <p> That earnest and nuanced answer was in its own way a distillation of the central issue regarding his leadership , since March 2016 , of one of the most esteemed editorial spaces in American journalism at a time when the space for polite disagreement seems to be shrinking rapidly . Bennet believes the editorials his team writes , and the op-ed columns he oversees , are about helping to recreate an intellectual and moral center in American public life . His version of the center is by no means a place in which everyone will agree with each other or split the difference on matters of fundamental belief . But it is one in which even people with strong views acknowledge the limits of their wisdom and welcome opposing perspectives , and arguments are intended as instruments of illumination . <p> There is an alternative view -- shared , as recent episodes have shown , even by some journalists within the Times -- that sees Bennet 's conception of the center as a place of moral dilution and even surrender . By these lights , in the America of Donald Trump and Fox News , arguments are instruments of power . If demagogues are willing to polarize on behalf of wrong-headed or even intentionally false arguments , it is folly for the Times and other establishment voices to not be equally polarizing on behalf of enlightened ones . <p> The controversies and Bennet 's views about an editor 's responsibility in an age of ideological and cultural combat were the subjects of our own recent conversation , excerpted below . <p> We did n't intend this as a traditional interview , with all the customary journalistic detachment that implies . Bennet and I have been friends for some 20 years . We like many of the same people , laugh at many of the same things . When we met , I was at the Washington Post , before leaving a decade later to start Politico ; he was then on his first tour at the Times , before leaving for a decade-long run as editor of the Atlantic . <p> The social media age has turned many journalists into radical individualists . Writers create their own brands and followings that do not depend so much on the publication they happen to work for . In Bennet 's case , all that upheaval has made him even more emphatically an institutionalist . <p> " I do feel -- like families -- institutions transmit values from one generation to another , " he said . " And that is really important . ... I think it 's really important that places like the New York Times make this transition . ... And I think it 's profoundly relevant to this world , even particularly at a time people do n't want to hear each other out if they disagree with each other . " <p> And yet Bennet , because he really does give a damn , has a hard time tuning out the haters . " You ca n't dismiss it , " he said . " You ca n't just say , ' Oh , they 're all a bunch of jackasses , ' because they 're not . But some of them are jackasses. " -- John F. Harris <p> *** <p> This conversation has been condensed and lightly edited for clarity . <p> John F. Harris : People know there is a big fuss about your leadership of the New York Times editorial page and its op-ed pages . From your vantage point , what is the fuss about ? <p> James Bennet : You 're probably in a better position to evaluate it than I am . I can tell you what we 're trying to do , which is to deliver on the core proposition of what Times opinion is supposed to be and has been supposed to be from the beginning , which I happen to think is particularly important and relevant in this day and age . Which is not to pretend that we 're in possession of the whole truth , and we all agree on what that truth is and about the way the world should be and what the right answers are to all of these huge questions that we 're facing , whether it 's on trade or immigration or how we all live together . But instead , we give people an honest struggle , an open debate from a lot of different points of view and show that you can do that kind of work respectfully , that you can actually engage across these different ideological divides and your -- even now , these days -- tribal divides . <p> Why is there such a fuss about it ? We exist in an incredibly hyperpartisan environment where the media is increasingly niche-ified and increasingly partisan and picking a side and shooting back and forth at each other between media organizations . And also because Donald Trump is president of the United States , and that makes a lot of people feel really , really vulnerable and afraid . And I get that . It makes it harder for people to hear an opposing point of view or a challenging point of view and with the same sense of security . I do n't know , what would you say ? Also , we 've made some mistakes that have pissed people off , so laughs , but I think -- <p> Harris : You wrote the memo to staff that was then widely circulated . Why did you write that ? Why did you feel it was necessary to write that ? What was the set of assumptions or perceptions that you were trying to address ? <p> Bennet : I have not done a good job of communicating inside or outside the Times about what our overall goals are and our ambitions . And that was an effort to improve on the communication . And I think there 's a lot of confusion and a lot of concern , including from colleagues at the New York Times and certainly outside the building . And there are people , you know , they encounter an opinion piece that they disagree with and it upsets them and they do n't understand how it fits into a larger conversation and debate , a kind of running debate in our pages . And I just felt I needed -- it was a moment where I needed to begin going on offense a little bit about what we 're trying to accomplish . <p> NOT AGREEING TO DISAGREE During the Trump administration , a familiar online pattern has emerged : a provocative , ( usually ) right-of-center New York Times op-ed followed by liberal anger setting social media and blogs aflame . Here are some of the biggest dust-ups . <p> Harris : And to that person that does n't understand , he or she might say , " This all sounds very reasonable , James , but the world is not reasonable , and the opponents of belief in facts , belief in fair-mindedness , belief in science , belief in rule of law , they 're not reasonable ; they 're not treating the game like it 's on the level . And here comes the New York Times editorial page pretending these are normal , reasonable , on-the-level times . " It 's like , " So you 're a sucker by playing the game as though the old rules exist . Which side are you on ? " I think it 's something like that . That 's maybe a fair paraphrase of what people would say ? <p> Bennet : What you 're describing is kind of the maximalist politics of the moment : " The other side is always going to make the maximalist demand , and if you 're talking about bipartisanship and compromise and so forth , you 're just going to get rolled , and the only way to win is to go in and fight that fight the same way . " OK , that 's fine . But that 's a political argument , you know ? That is not remotely a vision for a journalism that cares about the truth . Because the truth is almost definitionally , I do n't think , in the possession of partisans who are doing what you describe , making maximalist demands . The truth is something none of us is in possession of . None of us has all the right answers . And just as reporters go out there every day struggling to set their own assumptions aside and try to figure out what the facts are , the journalistic approach to opinion is to let people engage and argue things out . And that 's what I was trying to say in that email to colleagues . <p> Harris : There is not , as you describe it , a big gulf between traditional newsroom reporting values as opposed to editorial-page opinion values ; they 're both governed by a belief that we 're not in possession of all the facts and that there should be an ethos of kind of fair-mindedness and skepticism . <p> Bennet : Yes , in both places . I think there are basic principles that pertain in both worlds , right ? We care about fact first and foremost , getting it right . That 's kind of the basic commitment of all New York Times journalism . That means a high degree -- tremendous value placed on intellectual honesty and being willing to contend with reality . My kind of rough formula for the distinction is that the newsroom helps people see the world as it is , and opinion gets to help people imagine the world as it could be , how it could be made better , how you get to -- you know , that 's kind of the fun part of our work : We get to try to help figure out how to make the world a better place . So , there 's a degree of advocacy in opinion that differentiates it . <p> And there 's tons of overlap in all sorts of respects , obviously , because we 're reporting , the news side is reporting ; they do analysis , we do analysis . But at its core what differentiates us is our ability to advocate about what the right answers are . You 've got to be humble about that -- particularly now . It is a hyperpartisan moment , but at the same time our politics is really quite fluid . And you look at the Democrats and the Republicans -- you tell me what the Democrats ' foreign policy is or their trade policy . Or tell me the same on the Republican side . And there are a lot of big ideas , for example about trade , that are kind of up in the air right now , or , you know , should the tech companies be regulated ? How should they be regulated ? How do the parties think about it ? <p> James Bennet ( left ) and John Harris ( right ) at the New York Times headquarters in Manhattan . Ben Baker for Politico Magazine <p> We all kind of actually need to grope our way to the right answers to those questions . To pretend we know what they are now just seems ridiculous to me , but we need to figure them out . And our politics right now is not capable , does not feel -- I mean , you know better than me , but it sure does n't feel like they 're making a lot of progress toward answering those questions . And as opinion journalists , we owe it to our readers to try to help them figure it out , particularly at a moment when our politicians are not . <p> Harris : I think some people would argue that once you 've established facts and truth , the point of the spear should be pretty sharp , that this is not an environment that calls for soft arguments ; it calls for sharp and maybe even unyielding arguments because the other side is so unyielding . Paul Krugman would say , " Come on . The reasonable folks have been trumped by the unreasonable folks , so we should be -- we 're confident in our views . We should be just -- not unreasonable , but we should be unyielding , sharp , combative , defiant in our expression of them . " And maybe you 'd say that 's exactly what you 're trying to do with the page . Historically , editorials have had a kind of a certain judicious quality to them . Can that judiciousness be heard in the modern environment ? <p> Bennet : Once you have a high degree of conviction and you feel like the facts are on your side and you want to make a strong argument , I 've got no problem with that . I do think that even as you 're doing that you need to be -- again , with intellectual honesty as one of our core values , we have to be open-minded about hearing arguments on the other side and acknowledging it when the other side has a point on a given subject . So , I guess you can hear me talking out of both sides of my mouth on this one . Look , opinion writing is often pugilistic , and hopefully it 's entertaining and it 's fun and personable , because you 're hearing an individual 's voice . But yeah , I do worry a little bit that in this environment , particularly now , punching is not always the best way to get heard . It is the best way to rally the folks on your side often , but it 's not always the best way to reach people who are n't immediately inclined to agree with you . <p> Harris : Is there a generational signature to this ? You see it to some extent on campuses . People sometimes assert the right to be protected from viewpoints they find offensive . <p> Bennet : Yeah , there clearly is an element of that . I guess I 'm not panicked about that . I mean , obviously I 'm not happy about the people getting shouted down and not allowed to speak on campus . But I think -- and that concerns me because freedom of thought , freedom of expression is absolutely essential to what we care about here -- a lot of the campus stuff seems actually pretty positive , in the sense that part of it is about more speech and is about people who have n't really had their voices heard or been part of the debate or conversation coming into that conversation . <p> Harris : Many younger journalists at the Times or elsewhere are not that far removed from that campus environment . Do those people sort of fundamentally share the same journalistic values as you , or do they come from a different orientation ? <p> Bennet : I think all this stuff comes down to the person . Are there some journalists here or elsewhere , young journalists , who sort of think that the role of journalism in the Trump era is to be part of the Resistance ? Yeah , there probably are . And does that conflict with how I see the role of journalism ? Absolutely . So , I guess that is a clash of values , and I do worry about that a little bit . It 's just something we have to work out over time . <p> Harris : Does it bother you when people with whom you would assume you 're fundamentally of like minds and like values are really mad at you ? <p> Bennet : Oh , yeah . <p> Harris : It does ? Or do you just brush it off ? " It goes with the territory . " How much does it weigh on you ? <p> Bennet : Look , I do n't like to be called a Nazi , you know ? No , yeah , it -- <p> Harris : Who called you that ? <p> Bennet : Actually , I do n't know that I 've been -- I should subtract that . I 've been told I 've been called a Nazi ; I have not seen it . I should n't say that . That sounds ridiculous . I do n't know that anybody likes to be screamed at . Maybe there are people , but I 'm not one of them . And I take it seriously . Like , I take it to heart . Our posture is that we do n't have all the answers . And maybe I 'm wrong about what I 'm doing , and I have to hear the criticism . So , I take it seriously , and particularly when it comes from colleagues inside of the building . And to the extent that the criticism is constructive -- and a lot of it is -- it 's going to make us better over time if we hear it and act on it . But the hate -- the social media phenomenon where people are n't actually even reading the piece or engaging with the argument but they 're reacting to the tweet about the tweet about the tweet about the piece -- that sort of stuff makes me a little bit crazy . And , you know , I think our only option is you just kind of push through it . <p> Harris : Yeah . Maybe that 's an argument for not taking it that seriously . " Today 's shitstorm will be replaced by tomorrow 's shitstorm and another the day after that , and it 's folly to really follow it too closely or care very much . But , yeah , it does feel like the outrage machine is chewing its way day by day through one offense or another . And it 's really hard , I find , in this environment to sort out the signal and the noise . What is the important reaction , response , counterargument that we should be hearing ? It 's like the debate over free speech on campus , you know ? " Great . This is the whole point of debate . " This is the basic thing about engaging with people who disagree with you . It goes back to John Stuart Mill and arguments about liberty : You need to hear another point of view because you might be wrong or you might be right , but your ideas will get brittle if they 're not tested and you do n't have the argument . I think that 's what 's happening with free speech now ; the people who are advocates of free speech are having to remember why it 's so important and articulate that again . The courts are under stress . <p> It 's a little like what Tom Friedman says about the climate change , though : " OK , let 's say it 's not a problem . The aberrance of this moment did n't just arrive . Where does it end ? Or does it ? Maybe we just happen to be here at the end of Rome . And so , I think it makes us seem a little frivolous to be portraying ourselves on the front lines as though we 're freedom fighters . That 's in the press context . <p> In the citizenship context , I think democracy is really challenged at the moment .
